related_questions.question: What is the biggest cause of cancer?

text_blocks.snippet: The biggest preventable cause of cancer is tobacco use, specifically cigarette smoking. While many factors contribute to cancer development, tobacco use is strongly linked to a wide range of cancers, including lung cancer, and is responsible for a significant portion of cancer deaths.
Here's a breakdown of key points:

list.title: Tobacco use:
list.snippet: Cigarette smoking is the single biggest risk factor for lung cancer and is also linked to cancers of the mouth, throat, esophagus, stomach, colon, rectum, liver, pancreas, voice box, kidney, bladder, and cervix, as well as acute myeloid leukemia.

list.title: Other Risk Factors:
list.snippet: Other significant risk factors for cancer include:
Excess body weight/obesity: Being overweight or obese is a major risk factor for several cancers.
Alcohol consumption: Drinking alcohol increases the risk of various cancers.
UV radiation: Exposure to ultraviolet radiation from the sun or tanning beds is a major risk factor for skin cancer.
Lack of physical activity: Physical inactivity is linked to an increased risk of several cancers.
Diet: Diets high in red and processed meats and low in fruits and vegetables are associated with some cancers.
Infections: Certain viral and bacterial infections can increase cancer risk.

list.title: Preventability:
list.snippet: Many cancer cases and deaths are preventable by addressing modifiable risk factors like tobacco use, obesity, alcohol consumption, and lack of physical activity.

list.title: Genetic factors:
list.snippet: While genetic predisposition plays a role in some cancers, lifestyle and environmental factors are responsible for the majority of cancer cases.

text_blocks.snippet: Zantac (ranitidine) was found to contain unacceptable levels of N-nitrosodimethylamine (NDMA), a probable human carcinogen. This led to the FDA requesting a market withdrawal of all ranitidine products, including Zantac, in April 2020. While some studies suggested a link between ranitidine and certain cancers, particularly in the digestive system, others found no significant association with overall cancer risk.
snippet_highlighted_words: Zantac (ranitidine) was found to contain unacceptable levels of N-nitrosodimethylamine (NDMA), a probable human carcinogen

list.title: Carcinogen:
list.snippet: NDMA is a known carcinogen in animal studies and is classified as a probable human carcinogen.

list.title: FDA Recall:
list.snippet: The FDA requested the withdrawal of all ranitidine products from the market due to the presence of NDMA, which can increase to unacceptable levels, especially in older medications or those stored at high temperatures.

list.title: Increased Risk in Digestive System:
list.snippet: Some studies indicated a potential link between ranitidine use and increased risk of cancers in the gastric tract, including pharyngeal, esophageal, stomach, and colorectal cancers.

list.title: No Association with Overall Cancer Risk:
list.snippet: However, other studies, including a large multinational cohort study, found no significant association between ranitidine use and overall cancer risk.

list.title: Potential Link to Liver Cancer:
list.snippet: One study suggested a possible link between ranitidine use and liver cancer, but further research is needed to confirm this.

list.title: Need for Further Research:
list.snippet: Many studies acknowledge limitations, such as reliance on self-reported data, short follow-up periods, and potential for confounding factors, which highlight the need for more research to fully understand the long-term effects of ranitidine on cancer development.

list.title: Other H2RAs:
list.snippet: The FDA testing has not found NDMA in other H2 receptor antagonists like famotidine (Pepcid), cimetidine (Tagamet), and nizatidine.

list.title: Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs):
list.snippet: While PPIs like omeprazole (Prilosec) and esomeprazole (Nexium) are also used for acid reflux, some studies suggest long-term use may increase stomach cancer risk. It's important to discuss alternatives with a healthcare professional.
